reference.source: Congenital heart disease references / cardiology literature
clinicalPearls: An abnormal communication between a coronary artery and a cardiac chamber or great vessel, bypassing the myocardial capillary bed
Most are congenital, though some follow cardiac procedures or trauma
Many are small and asymptomatic, found incidentally on echocardiography or angiography as a continuous murmur
Large fistulae can cause a left-to-right shunt, coronary steal with ischaemia, heart failure or aneurysm formation
A continuous murmur, often atypical in location, is a clue
Small asymptomatic fistulae are observed; large or symptomatic ones are closed by catheter or surgery
reference.pathophysiology: A coronary arteriovenous fistula is a direct connection that shunts blood from a coronary artery into a low-pressure cardiac chamber or vein, diverting it from the myocardial capillary network. The shunt volume and drainage site determine the effects: diversion of coronary flow can cause a steal phenomenon with distal myocardial ischaemia, while a large left-to-right shunt increases volume load and can cause chamber dilatation and heart failure. Chronic high flow may lead to aneurysmal dilatation of the feeding coronary artery and predisposes to thrombosis.
additionalDifferentials: Anomalous origin of a coronary artery
additionalInvestigations: Coronary CT angiography or invasive coronary angiography to define the fistula
Assessment for ischaemia where coronary steal is suspected
redFlags: Angina or ischaemia from coronary steal
Heart failure from a large shunt
Endocarditis risk at the fistula site
reference.prognosis: Small fistulae often remain asymptomatic with a benign course, whereas large or symptomatic ones can cause ischaemia or heart failure and generally do well after catheter or surgical closure.
pitfalls: Attributing a continuous murmur solely to a patent ductus
Overlooking coronary steal as a cause of ischaemia
management: Manage small asymptomatic fistulae conservatively with periodic imaging surveillance
Close large or symptomatic fistulae definitively by transcatheter device occlusion or surgical ligation
Consider antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy where there is aneurysmal dilatation of the feeding artery or a high thrombotic risk, and after closure
Treat associated heart failure with diuretics and address myocardial ischaemia from coronary steal
Undertake surveillance echocardiography and cross-sectional imaging to monitor shunt size, aneurysm formation and residual flow after closure
Refer to a cardiology or congenital heart disease service for assessment and intervention planning
Escalate promptly if ischaemia, heart failure or aneurysmal complications develop
